notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Fertilizers are substances added to soil or plants to supply essential nutrients.
  • They improve plant growth and crop productivity when used correctly.
  • Fertilizers may be organic, inorganic, biological or combinations of these.
  • Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium are the three primary fertilizer nutrients.
  • They are commonly represented as N, P and K.
  • Excessive fertilizer application can damage soil, water and ecosystems.
  • Balanced fertilization is more important than simply applying large quantities of fertilizer.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Primary Fertilizer Nutrients → N + P + K

2. Essential Plant Nutrients

Modern plant science recognises 17 essential elements for higher plants.

They include:

  • Carbon.
  • Hydrogen.
  • Oxygen.
  • Nitrogen.
  • Phosphorus.
  • Potassium.
  • Calcium.
  • Magnesium.
  • Sulfur.
  • Iron.
  • Manganese.
  • Zinc.
  • Copper.
  • Boron.
  • Molybdenum.
  • Chlorine.
  • Nickel.
📌 TNPSC Note

Older textbooks may list 16 essential nutrients because nickel was recognised later as essential.

3. Carbon, Hydrogen and Oxygen
  • Plants obtain carbon mainly from atmospheric carbon dioxide.
  • Hydrogen is obtained mainly from water.
  • Oxygen comes from carbon dioxide, water and atmospheric oxygen.
  • These three elements form most of the dry matter of plants.
  • They are not normally supplied through conventional fertilizers.
4. Macronutrients

Macronutrients are required by plants in relatively large amounts.

They include:

  • Nitrogen.
  • Phosphorus.
  • Potassium.
  • Calcium.
  • Magnesium.
  • Sulfur.
5. Primary Macronutrients

Primary nutrients are:

  • Nitrogen → N.
  • Phosphorus → P.
  • Potassium → K.

They are called primary because crops remove large quantities of them and they commonly need replenishment.

📌 Must-Memorise

NPK → Nitrogen, Phosphorus, Potassium

6. Secondary Macronutrients

Secondary macronutrients are:

  • Calcium.
  • Magnesium.
  • Sulfur.
  • They are essential even though fertilizer discussions often focus mainly on NPK.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Secondary Nutrients → Ca + Mg + S

7. Micronutrients

Micronutrients are needed in very small quantities.

Important micronutrients are:

  • Iron.
  • Manganese.
  • Zinc.
  • Copper.
  • Boron.
  • Molybdenum.
  • Chlorine.
  • Nickel.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Micronutrients are needed in small amounts, but they are still essential.

8. Nitrogen — Role in Plants
  • Nitrogen is a major component of amino acids.
  • Amino acids form proteins.
  • Nitrogen is present in nucleic acids.
  • Nitrogen is a component of chlorophyll.
  • It promotes vegetative growth.
  • Leafy crops have particularly high nitrogen demand.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Nitrogen → Leafy/Vegetative Growth

9. Nitrogen Deficiency

Common symptoms include:

  • General chlorosis or yellowing.
  • Symptoms often appear first on older leaves.
  • Reduced growth.
  • Smaller leaves.
  • Early leaf fall in severe deficiency.
📌 Why Older Leaves?

Nitrogen is mobile within plants.

Plants can move nitrogen from older leaves to younger tissues.

10. Excess Nitrogen
  • Excess nitrogen can produce excessive vegetative growth.
  • Plants may become soft and prone to lodging.
  • Flowering or maturity may be delayed.
  • Pest and disease susceptibility can increase in some crops.
  • Excess nitrate can leach into groundwater.
11. Phosphorus — Role in Plants
  • Phosphorus is involved in energy transfer.
  • ATP contains phosphorus.
  • It is present in nucleic acids.
  • It promotes root growth.
  • It supports flowering and seed formation.
  • It is important for early plant development.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Phosphorus → Roots + Energy + Flowering

12. Phosphorus Deficiency

Symptoms may include:

  • Stunted growth.
  • Poor root development.
  • Delayed maturity.
  • Dark green foliage.
  • Purple or reddish pigmentation in some species.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Phosphorus Deficiency → Stunting + Purplish Leaves

13. Potassium — Role in Plants
  • Potassium regulates water balance.
  • It helps control stomatal opening.
  • It activates many enzymes.
  • It improves stress tolerance.
  • It supports disease resistance.
  • It improves crop quality and stem strength.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Potassium → Water Regulation + Stress Resistance

14. Potassium Deficiency

Typical symptoms include:

  • Yellowing or scorching at leaf margins.
  • Symptoms often appear first on older leaves.
  • Weak stems.
  • Poor resistance to drought and disease.
  • Reduced fruit and grain quality.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

K Deficiency → Leaf-Margin Scorching

15. Calcium
  • Calcium is important for cell-wall structure.
  • It stabilises cell membranes.
  • It supports root and shoot growing points.
  • Calcium is relatively immobile within plants.
  • Deficiency commonly affects young tissues.
16. Calcium Deficiency
  • Death of growing points may occur.
  • Young leaves can become distorted.
  • Poor root growth may occur.
  • Blossom-end rot of tomato is strongly associated with inadequate calcium supply to developing fruit.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Tomato Blossom-End Rot → Calcium Problem

17. Magnesium
  • Magnesium is the central atom in the chlorophyll molecule.
  • It is important for photosynthesis.
  • It activates many enzymes.
  • Magnesium is mobile within plants.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Magnesium → Chlorophyll

18. Magnesium Deficiency
  • Interveinal chlorosis commonly develops.
  • Older leaves are usually affected first.
  • Leaf veins may remain greener than surrounding tissue.
19. Sulfur
  • Sulfur is present in some amino acids.
  • Cysteine and methionine contain sulfur.
  • Sulfur is important in protein formation.
  • It also contributes to certain vitamins and coenzymes.
20. Sulfur Deficiency
  • Sulfur deficiency can cause general chlorosis.
  • Younger leaves often show symptoms first because sulfur is less mobile than nitrogen.
  • Plants may remain small and weak.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Nitrogen deficiency → Older leaves first.

Sulfur deficiency → Younger leaves often first.

21. Iron
  • Iron is required for chlorophyll synthesis processes.
  • It participates in electron transport.
  • It is essential for many enzymes.
  • Iron itself is not the central atom of chlorophyll.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Magnesium is at the centre of chlorophyll, not iron.

22. Iron Deficiency
  • Interveinal chlorosis appears mainly on young leaves.
  • Veins remain green while tissue between veins becomes yellow.
  • Iron deficiency is common in alkaline soils because iron becomes less available.
23. Zinc
  • Zinc activates many plant enzymes.
  • It influences growth hormones.
  • It is important for internode elongation.
  • Zinc deficiency is important in many agricultural soils.
24. Zinc Deficiency

Symptoms include:

  • Short internodes.
  • Small leaves.
  • Rosetting.
  • Interveinal chlorosis.
  • Stunted growth.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Zinc Deficiency → Little Leaf / Short Internodes

25. Boron
  • Boron is important in cell-wall development.
  • It supports growing points.
  • It is important in pollen formation and reproductive growth.
  • Both deficiency and excess can damage plants.
26. Molybdenum
  • Molybdenum is needed in very small amounts.
  • It is important for nitrate metabolism.
  • It is part of the nitrogenase enzyme system involved in biological nitrogen fixation.
  • Legumes require molybdenum for efficient symbiotic nitrogen fixation.
27. Nickel
  • Nickel is an essential micronutrient.
  • It is a component of the enzyme urease.
  • Urease helps metabolise urea.
  • Only very small quantities of nickel are required.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Nickel → Urease

28. Fertilizer
  • Fertilizer is a nutrient-rich material applied to soil or plants.
  • Fertilizers can supply one or many nutrients.
  • Chemical fertilizers generally contain nutrients in concentrated forms.
  • Fertilizer use should be based on crop and soil requirements.
29. Manure
  • Manure consists mainly of decomposed plant and animal wastes.
  • It contains nutrients in lower concentrations than most chemical fertilizers.
  • It adds organic matter to soil.
  • It improves soil structure.
  • It can improve water-holding capacity and microbial activity.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Manure → Nutrients + Organic Matter

30. Fertilizer vs Manure
  • Fertilizer → Concentrated nutrients.
  • Manure → Lower nutrient concentration.
  • Fertilizer → Usually quick nutrient availability.
  • Manure → Slower nutrient release.
  • Manure → Adds humus and improves soil structure.
  • Chemical fertilizer → Does not directly add significant organic matter.
31. Organic Fertilizers

Organic nutrient sources include:

  • Farmyard manure.
  • Compost.
  • Vermicompost.
  • Green manure.
  • Oil cakes.
  • Bone meal.
  • Poultry manure.
32. Farmyard Manure
  • FYM stands for Farmyard Manure.
  • It is made from cattle dung, urine, litter and farm wastes.
  • It adds organic matter.
  • Nutrient concentration is relatively low.
  • Well-decomposed FYM improves soil physical properties.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

FYM → Farmyard Manure

33. Compost
  • Compost is decomposed organic material.
  • Plant residues and biodegradable wastes are converted into humus-like material.
  • Microorganisms perform decomposition.
  • Compost supplies nutrients gradually.
  • It improves soil structure.
34. Vermicompost
  • Vermicompost is produced with the help of earthworms and microorganisms.
  • Earthworms fragment and process organic matter.
  • The product is rich in stabilised organic material.
  • Vermicompost can improve soil biological activity.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Vermicompost → Earthworms

35. Green Manure
  • Green-manure crops are grown and incorporated into soil while green.
  • They add organic matter.
  • Leguminous green-manure crops can add biologically fixed nitrogen.
  • Dhaincha and sunn hemp are commonly used examples.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Green Manure → Dhaincha + Sunn Hemp

36. Dhaincha
  • Dhaincha commonly refers to Sesbania species used for green manuring.
  • It grows rapidly.
  • It is incorporated into soil before maturity.
  • It adds biomass and nitrogen.
37. Oil Cakes
  • Oil cakes are residues remaining after oil extraction from seeds.
  • Groundnut cake, neem cake and mustard cake are examples.
  • They contain organic nutrients.
  • Some cakes are used as animal feed while others are used mainly as manure.
38. Neem Cake
  • Neem cake is a by-product of neem-oil extraction.
  • It can supply organic nutrients.
  • Neem compounds can suppress nitrification to some extent.
  • Neem products are also used in pest-management systems.
39. Chemical Fertilizers

Chemical fertilizers are manufactured nutrient salts or compounds.

They may be classified as:

  • Nitrogenous fertilizers.
  • Phosphatic fertilizers.
  • Potassic fertilizers.
  • Complex/compound fertilizers.
  • Mixed fertilizers.
  • Micronutrient fertilizers.
40. Nitrogenous Fertilizers

Common nitrogen fertilizers include:

  • Urea.
  • Ammonium sulfate.
  • Ammonium nitrate.
  • Calcium ammonium nitrate.
  • Ammonium chloride.
41. Urea
  • Chemical formula → CO(NH₂)₂.
  • Urea is the most concentrated common solid nitrogen fertilizer.
  • It contains about 46% nitrogen by mass.
  • It is highly soluble in water.
  • Urea is widely used throughout the world.
📌 Must-Memorise

Urea → 46% N

42. Urea in Soil
  • Urea is hydrolysed by the enzyme urease.
  • Ammonium forms after hydrolysis.
  • Soil microorganisms later convert ammonium to nitrate through nitrification.
  • Surface-applied urea can lose nitrogen as ammonia under unsuitable conditions.
43. Neem-Coated Urea
  • Neem coating slows some nitrogen transformations.
  • It can reduce rapid nitrification.
  • It can improve nitrogen-use efficiency under suitable conditions.
  • It also discourages diversion of agricultural urea for some non-agricultural purposes.
44. Ammonium Sulfate
  • Formula → (NH₄)₂SO₄.
  • It supplies nitrogen and sulfur.
  • It contains about 21% nitrogen.
  • It can acidify soil over repeated use.
  • It is useful for crops requiring sulfur.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ammonium Sulfate → N + S

45. Ammonium Nitrate
  • Formula → NH₄NO₃.
  • It contains nitrogen in both ammonium and nitrate forms.
  • It is a concentrated nitrogen fertilizer.
  • It is also a powerful oxidising material and requires strict safety controls.
46. Calcium Ammonium Nitrate
  • CAN stands for Calcium Ammonium Nitrate.
  • It supplies nitrogen.
  • It is less acidifying than some ammonium fertilizers because of calcium-containing material.
  • Commercial grades commonly contain around 26–27% nitrogen.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

CAN → Calcium Ammonium Nitrate

47. Ammonium Chloride
  • Formula → NH₄Cl.
  • It supplies nitrogen.
  • Its chloride content makes it unsuitable for chloride-sensitive crops when used excessively.
  • Repeated use can contribute to soil acidity.
48. Phosphatic Fertilizers

Important phosphatic fertilizers include:

  • Single superphosphate.
  • Triple superphosphate.
  • Diammonium phosphate.
  • Monoammonium phosphate.
  • Rock phosphate.
49. Single Superphosphate
  • SSP stands for Single Superphosphate.
  • It is produced by treating rock phosphate with sulfuric acid.
  • It supplies phosphorus.
  • It also supplies sulfur and calcium.
  • Common SSP contains roughly 16% available P₂O₅.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

SSP → P + S + Ca

50. Triple Superphosphate
  • TSP stands for Triple Superphosphate.
  • It is more concentrated in phosphorus than SSP.
  • It commonly contains about 46% P₂O₅.
  • It contains little or no sulfur compared with SSP.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

TSP → Concentrated Phosphatic Fertilizer

51. Rock Phosphate
  • Rock phosphate is a natural phosphorus-bearing mineral material.
  • It is a raw material for phosphatic fertilizer production.
  • Its direct effectiveness depends strongly on soil acidity and mineral characteristics.
  • It is more effective in acidic soils than strongly alkaline soils.
52. DAP
  • DAP stands for Diammonium Phosphate.
  • Formula → (NH₄)₂HPO₄.
  • It supplies both nitrogen and phosphorus.
  • Common fertilizer grade is 18-46-0.
  • This means approximately 18% N and 46% P₂O₅ equivalent.
📌 Must-Memorise

DAP → 18-46-0

53. MAP
  • MAP stands for Monoammonium Phosphate.
  • Formula → NH₄H₂PO₄.
  • It supplies nitrogen and phosphorus.
  • It is used in soil application and fertigation.
54. Potassic Fertilizers

Main potassic fertilizers include:

  • Muriate of Potash.
  • Sulfate of Potash.
  • Potassium is usually expressed in fertilizer grades as K₂O equivalent.
55. Muriate of Potash
  • MOP stands for Muriate of Potash.
  • Chemically, it is mainly potassium chloride.
  • Formula → KCl.
  • It is the most widely used potassic fertilizer.
  • Commercial MOP is commonly around 60% K₂O equivalent.
📌 Must-Memorise

MOP → KCl → ~60% K₂O

56. Sulfate of Potash
  • SOP stands for Sulfate of Potash.
  • Formula → K₂SO₄.
  • It supplies potassium and sulfur.
  • It is useful for chloride-sensitive crops.
  • It generally costs more than MOP.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

SOP → K + S, Low Chloride

57. Fertilizer Grade

Fertilizer grades are usually expressed as:

N – P₂O₅ – K₂O

Example:

18-46-0 means:

  • 18% nitrogen.
  • 46% phosphate expressed as P₂O₅.
  • 0% potash expressed as K₂O.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

The P and K values on fertilizer bags are conventionally expressed as P₂O₅ and K₂O equivalents, not elemental P and K.

58. NPK Fertilizer
  • NPK fertilizers supply nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
  • Different NPK grades contain different nutrient proportions.
  • Crop requirements determine the suitable NPK ratio.
  • Balanced fertilization means supplying nutrients according to need.
59. Straight Fertilizer
  • A straight fertilizer mainly supplies one primary plant nutrient.
  • Urea is primarily a nitrogen fertilizer.
  • MOP is primarily a potassium fertilizer.
  • SSP is primarily a phosphorus fertilizer though it also supplies sulfur and calcium.
60. Compound Fertilizer
  • Compound fertilizers contain two or more primary nutrients chemically combined or granulated together.
  • DAP supplies N and P.
  • Many NPK fertilizers contain N, P and K in each granule.
61. Mixed Fertilizer
  • Mixed fertilizers are physical mixtures of two or more fertilizer materials.
  • They can be prepared to achieve a desired nutrient ratio.
  • The nutrient distribution among individual granules may differ depending on manufacturing method.
62. Biofertilizer
  • Biofertilizers contain beneficial living microorganisms.
  • They improve nutrient availability.
  • They can fix nitrogen or solubilise nutrients.
  • They reduce dependence on chemical fertilizer when used appropriately.
  • Biofertilizers are not the same as manure.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Biofertilizer → Living Microorganisms

63. Biological Nitrogen Fixation
  • Atmospheric nitrogen is N₂.
  • Most plants cannot use atmospheric N₂ directly.
  • Certain microorganisms convert N₂ into biologically useful nitrogen compounds.
  • This is biological nitrogen fixation.
  • The enzyme nitrogenase is involved.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

N₂ → Usable Nitrogen → Nitrogen-Fixing Microorganisms

64. Nitrogenase
  • Nitrogenase enzyme catalyses biological nitrogen fixation.
  • It converts atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia.
  • It is highly sensitive to oxygen.
  • Molybdenum is an important component of many nitrogenase systems.
65. Rhizobium
  • Rhizobium bacteria form symbiotic associations with leguminous plants.
  • They occur in root nodules.
  • They fix atmospheric nitrogen.
  • Legumes receive usable nitrogen compounds.
  • Bacteria receive carbohydrates and a protected habitat.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rhizobium → Legume Root Nodules → Nitrogen Fixation

66. Leguminous Crops

Examples include:

  • Pea.
  • Bean.
  • Groundnut.
  • Gram.
  • Lentil.
  • Soybean.
  • Their roots can form nodules containing symbiotic nitrogen-fixing bacteria.
67. Azotobacter
  • Azotobacter is a free-living nitrogen-fixing bacterium.
  • It occurs in soil.
  • It does not require legume root nodules.
  • It is used as a biofertilizer for some non-leguminous crops.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Azotobacter → Free-Living N₂ Fixer

68. Azospirillum
  • Azospirillum is an associative nitrogen-fixing bacterium.
  • It is associated with roots of grasses and cereals.
  • It is widely used as a biofertilizer.
  • It is especially relevant to crops such as rice, maize and millets.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Azospirillum → Cereals/Grasses

69. Cyanobacteria
  • Some cyanobacteria can fix atmospheric nitrogen.
  • Examples include Anabaena and Nostoc.
  • They are particularly important in wetland rice cultivation.
  • They were historically called blue-green algae.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Anabaena + Nostoc → Nitrogen-Fixing Cyanobacteria

70. Azolla
  • Azolla is a small aquatic fern.
  • It contains symbiotic nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria, traditionally called Anabaena azollae.
  • Azolla is used as a biofertilizer in paddy fields.
  • It can also contribute organic matter.
📌 Must-Memorise

Azolla + Anabaena → Paddy Biofertilizer

71. Mycorrhiza
  • Mycorrhiza is a symbiotic association between fungi and plant roots.
  • The fungus increases effective root-absorbing area.
  • It is especially useful for phosphorus uptake.
  • Plants provide carbohydrates to the fungus.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mycorrhiza → Better Phosphorus Uptake

72. Phosphate-Solubilising Microorganisms
  • Some bacteria and fungi convert poorly soluble phosphate into more plant-available forms.
  • Bacillus and Pseudomonas species are commonly cited.
  • Such organisms are used as phosphate-solubilising biofertilizers.
73. Nitrogen Cycle

Major processes include:

  • Nitrogen fixation.
  • Ammonification.
  • Nitrification.
  • Assimilation.
  • Denitrification.
74. Nitrogen Fixation
  • Nitrogen fixation converts atmospheric N₂ into ammonia or related usable forms.
  • It can occur biologically.
  • Lightning can also fix small amounts of nitrogen.
  • Industrial fixation occurs through the Haber-Bosch process.
75. Ammonification
  • Decomposers break down organic nitrogen compounds.
  • Ammonia or ammonium is produced.
  • This process is called ammonification.
  • Bacteria and fungi participate.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Organic Nitrogen → NH₃/NH₄⁺ = Ammonification

76. Nitrification
  • Nitrification converts ammonium into nitrate through microbial oxidation.
  • It usually occurs in two main steps.
  • Ammonium → Nitrite.
  • Nitrite → Nitrate.
77. Nitrosomonas
  • In classical school-level nitrogen-cycle descriptions, Nitrosomonas converts ammonia/ammonium into nitrite.
  • It is a nitrifying bacterium.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Nitrosomonas → NH₄⁺ to NO₂⁻

78. Nitrobacter
  • In traditional textbook descriptions, Nitrobacter converts nitrite into nitrate.
  • Nitrate is readily taken up by many plants.
  • Modern microbiology also recognises other important nitrite oxidisers such as Nitrospira.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Nitrobacter → NO₂⁻ to NO₃⁻

79. Denitrification
  • Denitrification converts nitrate into gaseous nitrogen forms.
  • It occurs mainly under low-oxygen conditions.
  • It returns nitrogen to the atmosphere.
  • Pseudomonas species are commonly associated with denitrification.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Denitrification → Nitrate → Atmospheric N₂

80. Assimilation
  • Plants absorb nitrate or ammonium from soil.
  • They convert the nitrogen into amino acids and other organic molecules.
  • Animals obtain nitrogen by consuming plants or other animals.
81. Haber-Bosch Process
  • The Haber-Bosch process manufactures ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen.
  • Nitrogen is obtained from air.
  • Hydrogen is commonly obtained industrially from natural gas or other sources.
  • The process uses high temperature, high pressure and an iron-based catalyst.
📌 Reaction

N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃

🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Haber Process → Ammonia

82. Haber Process Conditions

Typical industrial conditions are approximately:

  • Temperature → Around 400–500°C.
  • Pressure → Roughly 150–250 atmospheres in many plants.
  • Catalyst → Iron-based catalyst.
📌 Must-Memorise

Haber → N₂ + H₂ → NH₃ → Iron Catalyst

83. Fritz Haber
  • Fritz Haber developed the laboratory method for synthesising ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen.
  • He received the 1918 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
  • Industrial ammonia production transformed fertilizer manufacture.
84. Carl Bosch
  • Carl Bosch developed large-scale high-pressure industrial production of ammonia.
  • He adapted Haber's process for industry.
  • He shared the 1931 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Friedrich Bergius.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Haber → Chemistry of NH₃ synthesis

Bosch → Industrial Scale-Up

85. Ammonia and Fertilizers

Ammonia is used to manufacture:

  • Urea.
  • Ammonium sulfate.
  • Ammonium nitrate.
  • DAP.
  • MAP.
  • Nitric acid for fertilizer production.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

NH₃ → Foundation of Nitrogen Fertilizer Industry

86. Urea Production
  • Industrial urea is manufactured mainly from ammonia and carbon dioxide.
  • Both are reacted under high pressure.
  • Urea provides highly concentrated nitrogen.
📌 Simplified Overall Reaction

2NH₃ + CO₂ → CO(NH₂)₂ + H₂O

87. Phosphate Fertilizer Production
  • Phosphate rock is the main mineral raw material.
  • Sulfuric acid or phosphoric acid is used to convert insoluble rock phosphate into more soluble fertilizer forms.
  • SSP, TSP, DAP and MAP are major products.
88. Potash
  • Potash is a general term for potassium-containing fertilizer materials.
  • Potassium chloride is the main commercial source.
  • Potash fertilizer grades are expressed as K₂O equivalent.
89. Soil Fertility
  • Soil fertility is the capacity of soil to supply essential nutrients in suitable amounts.
  • Fertility depends on nutrient reserves, organic matter, pH and biological activity.
  • Fertility is only one part of soil productivity.
90. Soil Productivity
  • Soil productivity refers to the ability of soil to produce crops under particular management.
  • Productivity depends on fertility plus water, climate, structure, pests and management.
  • A fertile soil may still have low productivity if water or climate is unsuitable.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Soil fertility ≠ Soil productivity.

91. Soil Organic Matter
  • Organic matter improves soil aggregation.
  • It increases water-holding capacity.
  • It supports microorganisms.
  • It provides slowly released nutrients.
  • It improves cation-exchange capacity in many soils.
92. Humus
  • Humus is stable, decomposed organic material in soil.
  • It is dark coloured.
  • It improves soil structure.
  • It helps retain water and nutrients.
  • Humus forms slowly through decomposition.
93. Soil pH and Nutrients
  • Soil pH strongly affects nutrient availability.
  • Very acidic or very alkaline soils can make some nutrients unavailable.
  • Most crops perform well in mildly acidic to neutral soils, though optimum pH varies by crop.
  • Soil testing helps guide liming and fertilizer use.
94. Acidic Soil and Fertilizers
  • Ammonium-based fertilizers can gradually acidify soil.
  • Repeated use without correction may lower pH.
  • Lime is used to neutralise excessive soil acidity.
  • Calcium carbonate is a common liming material.
95. Alkaline Soil
  • Highly alkaline soils can reduce availability of iron, zinc and phosphorus.
  • Corrective management depends on the cause.
  • Gypsum is often used for sodic soils, where excessive exchangeable sodium is a problem.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Sodic Soil → Gypsum Common Amendment

96. Gypsum in Agriculture
  • Gypsum formula → CaSO₄·2H₂O.
  • It supplies calcium and sulfur.
  • It can help reclaim sodic soils.
  • Calcium replaces sodium on soil exchange sites.
97. Liming
  • Liming means adding basic materials to acidic soil.
  • Limestone → CaCO₃.
  • Quicklime → CaO.
  • Slaked lime → Ca(OH)₂.
  • Agricultural limestone is commonly used because it is safer and easier to handle than quicklime.
98. Soil Testing
  • Soil testing measures nutrient status and pH.
  • It helps determine suitable fertilizer doses.
  • It prevents both deficiency and excessive application.
  • Fertilizer recommendation should consider crop requirement and expected yield.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Soil Test → Scientific Fertilizer Recommendation

99. Balanced Fertilization
  • Balanced fertilization supplies nutrients in the correct proportion.
  • Applying nitrogen alone cannot compensate for phosphorus or potassium deficiency.
  • Secondary and micronutrients must also be supplied when deficient.
  • Balanced nutrition improves nutrient-use efficiency.
100. Integrated Nutrient Management
  • INM stands for Integrated Nutrient Management.
  • It combines chemical fertilizers, organic manures and biofertilizers.
  • The goal is to maintain productivity while protecting soil health.
  • Crop residues and green manures may also be included.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

INM → Chemical + Organic + Biological Sources

101. Fertigation
  • Fertigation is application of dissolved fertilizers through irrigation water.
  • It is common in drip-irrigation systems.
  • Nutrients can be supplied in smaller, frequent doses.
  • Fertigation can improve fertilizer-use efficiency when managed correctly.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Fertigation → Fertilizer + Irrigation

102. Foliar Fertilization
  • Foliar fertilization means spraying nutrients on leaves.
  • Micronutrients are often efficiently supplied through foliar sprays.
  • It can correct some deficiencies rapidly.
  • It does not replace all soil nutrient requirements.
103. Basal Application
  • Basal fertilizer is applied before or at sowing/transplanting.
  • Phosphorus and potassium are often substantially applied as basal doses.
  • Placement near the root zone can improve efficiency.
104. Top Dressing
  • Top dressing means applying fertilizer to a growing crop after establishment.
  • Nitrogen is commonly applied in split top dressings.
  • Splitting nitrogen reduces losses and better matches crop demand.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Top Dressing → Commonly Nitrogen

105. Split Application
  • The total fertilizer dose is divided into several applications.
  • Split nitrogen application can reduce leaching and volatilisation losses.
  • It supplies nutrient closer to the period of crop demand.
106. Fertilizer Placement
  • Fertilizer may be broadcast over the field.
  • It may be placed in bands.
  • It may be drilled near seed rows.
  • Placement affects nutrient efficiency.
  • Phosphorus is relatively immobile and often benefits from proper placement.
107. Nitrogen Loss — Leaching
  • Nitrate is highly soluble.
  • It can move downward with drainage water.
  • This is called nitrate leaching.
  • Excess fertilizer increases groundwater contamination risk.
108. Nitrogen Loss — Volatilisation
  • Ammonia gas can be lost from surface-applied urea.
  • Loss is greater under warm, alkaline and moist surface conditions.
  • Incorporating urea or applying before suitable irrigation can reduce losses.
109. Nitrogen Loss — Denitrification
  • Under waterlogged, oxygen-poor conditions, nitrate can be converted to gaseous nitrogen.
  • Nitrogen is then lost to the atmosphere.
  • Nitrous oxide may also be released.
110. Nitrous Oxide
  • Nitrous oxide formula → N₂O.
  • It is a powerful greenhouse gas.
  • Agricultural soils receiving nitrogen fertilizer are an important anthropogenic source.
  • Nitrification and denitrification contribute to N₂O emissions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Excess Nitrogen Fertilization → N₂O Emissions

111. Phosphorus Fixation
  • Soil phosphorus can react with minerals and become less available.
  • In acidic soils it can bind strongly with iron and aluminium.
  • In alkaline soils it can precipitate with calcium.
  • Phosphorus therefore moves relatively little in most soils.
112. Potassium Fixation
  • Some clay minerals can trap potassium between layers.
  • This reduces immediate availability.
  • Potassium can later be released slowly.
  • Soil mineralogy affects potassium behaviour.
113. Nutrient-Use Efficiency
  • Nutrient-use efficiency is the proportion of applied nutrient successfully used by crops.
  • Losses occur through leaching, volatilisation, runoff, erosion and chemical fixation.
  • Correct timing, placement and dose improve efficiency.
114. Slow-Release Fertilizer
  • Slow-release fertilizers supply nutrients gradually.
  • They reduce rapid nutrient loss.
  • Polymer-coated fertilizers are one example.
  • They can reduce the frequency of fertilizer application.
115. Controlled-Release Fertilizer
  • Controlled-release fertilizers are designed to release nutrients at a predictable rate.
  • Coatings regulate water penetration and nutrient diffusion.
  • They can improve nutrient-use efficiency but are generally more expensive.
116. Nitrification Inhibitors
  • Nitrification inhibitors slow microbial conversion of ammonium into nitrate.
  • They can reduce nitrate leaching.
  • They may also reduce some nitrous-oxide emissions.
  • Neem compounds can have nitrification-inhibiting effects.
117. Urease Inhibitors
  • Urease inhibitors slow the conversion of urea to ammonium.
  • They can reduce ammonia volatilisation from surface-applied urea.
  • Their use can improve nitrogen efficiency under suitable conditions.
118. Fertilizer and Eutrophication
  • Excess nitrogen and phosphorus can enter lakes and rivers.
  • Nutrient enrichment causes excessive algal growth.
  • This process is called eutrophication.
  • Decomposition of algae consumes dissolved oxygen.
  • Fish kills may occur under severe oxygen depletion.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Excess N + P → Eutrophication

119. Algal Bloom
  • An algal bloom is rapid growth of algae or cyanobacteria.
  • Nutrient-rich water promotes blooms.
  • Some blooms produce toxins.
  • Dense blooms can block light and reduce oxygen.
120. Groundwater Nitrate Pollution
  • Excess nitrate can leach into groundwater.
  • High nitrate in drinking water is a health concern.
  • Infants are particularly vulnerable to methemoglobinemia.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Nitrate Pollution → Blue-Baby Syndrome Risk

121. Methemoglobinemia
  • Methemoglobinemia reduces haemoglobin's ability to carry oxygen effectively.
  • High nitrate exposure is a known risk factor in infants.
  • It is sometimes called blue-baby syndrome in this context.
122. Soil Salinity
  • Excessive fertilizer salts can increase soil salinity.
  • Salinity makes water uptake harder for plants.
  • Sensitive crops can suffer reduced growth.
  • Good irrigation and drainage management are important in saline areas.
123. Soil Acidification
  • Repeated use of some ammonium nitrogen fertilizers can lower soil pH.
  • Acidification can increase aluminium toxicity in strongly acidic soils.
  • Liming may be required.
124. Fertilizer Burn
  • Highly concentrated fertilizer near seeds or roots can draw water out of plant tissues.
  • Salt injury may damage seedlings.
  • Excess ammonia can also injure plants.
  • Correct rate and placement prevent fertilizer burn.
125. Organic Agriculture and Fertility
  • Organic systems rely strongly on manure, compost, green manures, rotations and biological nutrient cycling.
  • Legumes contribute nitrogen through symbiotic fixation.
  • Organic fertilizers still contain chemical nutrients; “organic” describes source and production system, not absence of chemicals.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Organic manure still contains chemical elements such as N, P and K.

126. Crop Rotation
  • Crop rotation means growing different crops in sequence.
  • Legume inclusion can improve soil nitrogen status.
  • Rotation can also reduce pest and disease buildup.
  • It improves nutrient-use patterns.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Legume Rotation → Nitrogen Benefit

127. Legumes and Nitrogen Fertilizer
  • Legumes can obtain much of their nitrogen through Rhizobium symbiosis.
  • Effective nodulation reduces the requirement for external nitrogen fertilizer.
  • Phosphorus and other nutrients are still required.
128. Paddy Fields and Biofertilizers

Important biofertilizers for rice include:

  • Azospirillum.
  • Cyanobacteria.
  • Azolla-associated cyanobacteria.
  • Flooded paddy conditions favour specific biological nutrient cycles.
129. Micronutrient Fertilizers

Examples include:

  • Zinc sulfate.
  • Ferrous sulfate.
  • Borax.
  • Copper sulfate.
  • Sodium molybdate or ammonium molybdate.
  • They are applied in small quantities.
130. Zinc Sulfate
  • Zinc sulfate is widely used to correct zinc deficiency.
  • Zinc deficiency is common in rice and several other crops.
  • Excess zinc, however, can also be toxic.
131. Borax
  • Borax supplies boron.
  • Boron is required only in very small amounts.
  • The difference between deficiency and toxicity can be narrow.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Micronutrient → More is not necessarily better.

132. Chelated Micronutrients
  • Chelates hold metal ions in soluble forms.
  • Iron, zinc and other micronutrients can be supplied as chelates.
  • Chelation can improve nutrient availability, especially in alkaline soils.
133. Fertilizer Production and Energy
  • Nitrogen fertilizer production is energy intensive.
  • Haber-Bosch ammonia production requires hydrogen.
  • Natural gas is currently a major source of both hydrogen and process energy.
  • Therefore nitrogen fertilizer prices are closely linked to energy costs.
134. Green Ammonia
  • Ammonia can be produced using hydrogen generated by renewable-powered electrolysis.
  • This is commonly called green ammonia when associated emissions are very low.
  • The ammonia molecule is chemically the same regardless of hydrogen source.
135. Nitrogen Fertilizer and Climate
  • Ammonia production can release significant CO₂ when hydrogen is made from fossil fuels.
  • Field application can release nitrous oxide.
  • Improving nitrogen efficiency can reduce environmental impact.
136. Fertilizer Storage
  • Fertilizers should be kept dry.
  • Moisture can cause caking and deterioration.
  • Ammonium nitrate requires particularly strict safety controls.
  • Fertilizers should be stored away from food and feed.
137. Hygroscopic Fertilizers
  • Hygroscopic substances absorb moisture from air.
  • Some fertilizers readily become damp or caked.
  • Proper sealed storage is therefore important.
138. Fertilizer Compatibility
  • Not all fertilizers should be mixed and stored together.
  • Some combinations react chemically or absorb moisture.
  • Fertilizer mixtures should follow agronomic compatibility guidelines.
139. Important Fertilizer Formulae
  • Urea → CO(NH₂)₂.
  • Ammonium sulfate → (NH₄)₂SO₄.
  • Ammonium nitrate → NH₄NO₃.
  • DAP → (NH₄)₂HPO₄.
  • MAP → NH₄H₂PO₄.
  • MOP → KCl.
  • SOP → K₂SO₄.
  • Gypsum → CaSO₄·2H₂O.
140. Important Fertilizer Numbers
  • Urea → ~46% N.
  • Ammonium sulfate → ~21% N.
  • DAP → 18-46-0.
  • SSP → ~16% P₂O₅.
  • TSP → ~46% P₂O₅.
  • MOP → ~60% K₂O equivalent.
  • CAN → commonly ~26–27% N.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Urea 46

DAP 18-46-0

MOP 60

141. Scientist–Fact Pairs
  • Fritz Haber → Ammonia synthesis.
  • Carl Bosch → Industrial high-pressure ammonia production.
  • Martinus Beijerinck → Important early work on nitrogen-fixing microorganisms, including isolation/study of Azotobacter.
  • Sergei Winogradsky → Major work on nitrifying bacteria and soil microbiology.
142. Must-Memorise Nutrient Roles
  • Nitrogen → Leaves/protein/chlorophyll.
  • Phosphorus → Roots/ATP/flowers.
  • Potassium → Water balance/stress tolerance.
  • Calcium → Cell walls/growing points.
  • Magnesium → Chlorophyll.
  • Sulfur → Sulfur amino acids.
  • Iron → Chlorophyll formation/electron transport.
  • Zinc → Enzymes/growth.
  • Molybdenum → Nitrogen metabolism/fixation.
143. Must-Memorise Deficiency Links
  • N deficiency → Older leaves yellow.
  • P deficiency → Stunting/purple colour.
  • K deficiency → Leaf-margin scorching.
  • Mg deficiency → Interveinal chlorosis on older leaves.
  • Fe deficiency → Interveinal chlorosis on young leaves.
  • Zn deficiency → Small leaves/short internodes.
  • S deficiency → Young leaves yellow.
  • Ca deficiency → Growing-point injury.
144. Must-Memorise Biofertilizer Links
  • Rhizobium → Legumes.
  • Azotobacter → Free-living nitrogen fixer.
  • Azospirillum → Cereals/grasses.
  • Anabaena → Cyanobacterial nitrogen fixer.
  • Nostoc → Cyanobacterial nitrogen fixer.
  • Azolla → Paddy.
  • Mycorrhiza → Phosphorus uptake.
145. Must-Memorise Nitrogen-Cycle Links
  • Nitrogen fixation → N₂ to NH₃.
  • Ammonification → Organic N to NH₃/NH₄⁺.
  • Nitrification → NH₄⁺ to NO₃⁻.
  • Nitrosomonas → NH₄⁺ to NO₂⁻.
  • Nitrobacter → NO₂⁻ to NO₃⁻.
  • Denitrification → NO₃⁻ to N₂.
  • Pseudomonas → Common denitrifier.
146. TNPSC Traps
  • NPK means nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
  • Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen are essential but usually not fertilizer nutrients.
  • Micronutrients are essential despite being required in small amounts.
  • Magnesium is the central atom in chlorophyll.
  • Iron is not the central atom in chlorophyll.
  • Nitrogen deficiency generally appears first on older leaves.
  • Iron deficiency generally appears first on young leaves.
  • Urea contains about 46% nitrogen.
  • DAP grade is commonly 18-46-0.
  • DAP supplies N and P, not potassium.
  • MOP is potassium chloride.
  • MOP mainly supplies potassium, not phosphorus.
  • SSP supplies phosphorus plus sulfur and calcium.
  • Fertilizer-grade P is expressed as P₂O₅ equivalent.
  • Fertilizer-grade K is expressed as K₂O equivalent.
  • Biofertilizer contains living microorganisms.
  • Rhizobium is associated with legume root nodules.
  • Azotobacter is free living.
  • Azospirillum is associated with grasses/cereals.
  • Azolla is especially associated with paddy.
  • Mycorrhiza helps phosphorus uptake.
  • Haber process produces ammonia, not urea directly.
  • Urea is manufactured from ammonia and carbon dioxide.
  • Nitrosomonas → Nitrite formation.
  • Nitrobacter → Nitrate formation in classical textbook treatment.
  • Denitrification returns nitrogen to the atmosphere.
  • Phosphorus is relatively immobile in soil.
  • Excess fertilizer can cause eutrophication.
  • Excess nitrate can contaminate groundwater.
  • Excess ammonium fertilizer can acidify soil.
  • Gypsum is used in reclamation of sodic soil.
  • Lime is used for acidic soil.
  • Fertigation means fertilizer through irrigation.
  • Top dressing commonly involves nitrogen.
  • Organic manure is not nutrient-free.
  • Soil fertility and soil productivity are not identical.
147. Ultra-Short Memory Chain
  • NPK → Primary nutrients.
  • N → Leaves.
  • P → Roots.
  • K → Stress resistance.
  • Mg → Chlorophyll.
  • Urea → 46% N.
  • DAP → 18-46-0.
  • MOP → KCl.
  • SSP → P + S.
  • TSP → Concentrated P.
  • FYM → Farmyard manure.
  • Vermicompost → Earthworms.
  • Green manure → Dhaincha.
  • Biofertilizer → Microorganisms.
  • Rhizobium → Legume.
  • Azotobacter → Free living.
  • Azospirillum → Cereals.
  • Azolla → Paddy.
  • Mycorrhiza → P uptake.
  • Haber → Ammonia.
  • Nitrosomonas → Nitrite.
  • Nitrobacter → Nitrate.
  • Pseudomonas → Denitrification.
  • Acidic soil → Lime.
  • Sodic soil → Gypsum.
  • Excess N/P → Eutrophication.
  • Fertigation → Fertilizer + irrigation.
Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected
  • What are fertilizers? → Materials supplying plant nutrients.
  • Three primary plant nutrients? → Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
  • NPK stands for? → Nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium.
  • Primary macronutrients? → N, P and K.
  • Secondary macronutrients? → Calcium, magnesium and sulfur.
  • Modern number of essential plant elements? → 17.
  • Three essential elements obtained mainly from air/water? → Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
  • Nitrogen mainly promotes? → Vegetative and leafy growth.
  • Nitrogen is part of? → Proteins, nucleic acids and chlorophyll.
  • Nitrogen deficiency first appears mainly where? → Older leaves.
  • Main symptom of nitrogen deficiency? → General yellowing/chlorosis.
  • Phosphorus mainly supports? → Root growth, energy transfer and flowering.
  • Phosphorus deficiency may cause? → Stunting and purplish coloration.
  • Potassium mainly helps? → Water regulation and stress/disease resistance.
  • Potassium deficiency typically causes? → Leaf-margin scorching.
  • Central atom of chlorophyll? → Magnesium.
  • Iron deficiency commonly causes? → Interveinal chlorosis of young leaves.
  • Magnesium deficiency commonly affects? → Older leaves.
  • Micronutrient associated with urease? → Nickel.
  • Micronutrient important for nitrogenase? → Molybdenum.
  • Fertilizer vs manure? → Fertilizer is concentrated nutrient source; manure also adds organic matter.
  • FYM stands for? → Farmyard Manure.
  • Vermicompost produced using? → Earthworms.
  • Common green-manure crops? → Dhaincha and sunn hemp.
  • Chemical formula of urea? → CO(NH₂)₂.
  • Nitrogen percentage in urea? → About 46%.
  • Ammonium sulfate formula? → (NH₄)₂SO₄.
  • Ammonium sulfate supplies? → Nitrogen and sulfur.
  • CAN stands for? → Calcium Ammonium Nitrate.
  • SSP stands for? → Single Superphosphate.
  • SSP supplies? → Phosphorus, sulfur and calcium.
  • Approximate P₂O₅ in SSP? → About 16%.
  • TSP stands for? → Triple Superphosphate.
  • Approximate P₂O₅ in TSP? → About 46%.
  • DAP stands for? → Diammonium Phosphate.
  • DAP formula? → (NH₄)₂HPO₄.
  • Common DAP grade? → 18-46-0.
  • Does DAP supply potassium? → No.
  • MAP stands for? → Monoammonium Phosphate.
  • MOP stands for? → Muriate of Potash.
  • MOP chemical formula? → KCl.
  • MOP supplies? → Potassium.
  • Approximate MOP grade? → About 60% K₂O equivalent.
  • SOP stands for? → Sulfate of Potash.
  • SOP formula? → K₂SO₄.
  • SOP supplies? → Potassium and sulfur.
  • Fertilizer grade written as? → N-P₂O₅-K₂O.
  • What does 18-46-0 mean? → 18% N, 46% P₂O₅, 0% K₂O.
  • What is a biofertilizer? → Preparation containing beneficial living microorganisms.
  • Bacterium in legume root nodules? → Rhizobium.
  • Function of Rhizobium? → Nitrogen fixation.
  • Free-living nitrogen-fixing bacterium? → Azotobacter.
  • Associative nitrogen fixer used with cereals? → Azospirillum.
  • Nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria? → Anabaena and Nostoc.
  • Aquatic fern used as paddy biofertilizer? → Azolla.
  • Azolla's symbiotic nitrogen fixer? → Anabaena-type cyanobacterium.
  • Mycorrhiza improves uptake mainly of? → Phosphorus.
  • Enzyme responsible for biological nitrogen fixation? → Nitrogenase.
  • Nitrogen fixation converts? → N₂ into ammonia/us­able nitrogen.
  • Ammonification converts? → Organic nitrogen into ammonia/ammonium.
  • Nitrification converts? → Ammonium into nitrate.
  • Nitrosomonas converts? → Ammonium to nitrite.
  • Nitrobacter converts? → Nitrite to nitrate in standard textbook treatment.
  • Denitrification converts? → Nitrate to gaseous nitrogen.
  • Common denitrifying bacterium? → Pseudomonas.
  • Industrial process for ammonia? → Haber-Bosch process.
  • Haber reaction? → N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃.
  • Haber catalyst? → Iron-based catalyst.
  • Approximate Haber temperature? → Around 400–500°C.
  • Why is high pressure used in Haber process? → It favours ammonia formation and increases reaction rate.
  • Scientists associated with ammonia process? → Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch.
  • Urea manufactured mainly from? → Ammonia and carbon dioxide.
  • Raw material for phosphatic fertilizers? → Rock phosphate.
  • Main raw material for potassic fertilizer MOP? → Potassium chloride-bearing potash minerals.
  • What is soil fertility? → Ability of soil to supply essential nutrients.
  • Is soil fertility same as productivity? → No.
  • Stable decomposed soil organic matter? → Humus.
  • How does soil pH affect plants? → It controls nutrient availability.
  • Treatment for acidic soil? → Lime.
  • Common amendment for sodic soil? → Gypsum.
  • Gypsum formula? → CaSO₄·2H₂O.
  • INM stands for? → Integrated Nutrient Management.
  • INM combines? → Chemical fertilizers, organic manures and biofertilizers.
  • Fertigation means? → Fertilizer application through irrigation water.
  • Foliar fertilization means? → Nutrient application to leaves.
  • Top dressing commonly supplies? → Nitrogen.
  • Why is nitrogen often split into several doses? → To match crop demand and reduce losses.
  • Major nitrate loss from soil? → Leaching.
  • Ammonia loss from surface urea called? → Volatilisation.
  • Nitrogen loss under waterlogged conditions? → Denitrification.
  • Important greenhouse gas linked to nitrogen fertilizer? → Nitrous oxide, N₂O.
  • Why is phosphorus relatively immobile? → It becomes chemically fixed or precipitated in soil.
  • What is eutrophication? → Excess nutrient enrichment of water causing algal growth.
  • Main agricultural nutrients causing eutrophication? → Nitrogen and phosphorus.
  • Effect of severe algal bloom decomposition? → Dissolved oxygen falls.
  • Groundwater nitrate can cause which infant condition? → Methemoglobinemia or blue-baby syndrome.
  • Can excessive fertilizer harm crops? → Yes, through salt injury and nutrient imbalance.
  • What is fertilizer burn? → Root/seed injury from excessive fertilizer concentration.
  • Crop rotation with legumes helps mainly by? → Increasing biologically fixed nitrogen.
  • Important paddy biofertilizers? → Azolla, cyanobacteria and Azospirillum.
  • Common fertilizer for zinc deficiency? → Zinc sulfate.
  • Does micronutrient mean unimportant nutrient? → No.
  • Does more micronutrient always improve growth? → No; excess can be toxic.
  • Core TNPSC memory line? → Urea → 46% N; DAP → 18-46-0; MOP → KCl; Rhizobium → legumes; Azolla → paddy; Mycorrhiza → phosphorus; Nitrosomonas → nitrite; Nitrobacter → nitrate.
